turnover.title: Turnover (fees and sales)
turnover.summary: Turnover is all the money your business earns before any expenses. It is income, not an expense. On the cash basis (the default from 2024-25) you count it when the money reaches you; on traditional accounting you count it when the work is done and invoiced.
rules: Include every payment for your work: day rates, fees, overtime, tips, commissions and payments in kind.
Include money clients pay you to cover your costs (recharges, per diems, buyouts). Then claim the real allowable costs as expenses.
Cash basis: record the income on the date you are paid, not the PO date or invoice date.
Traditional accounting: include work done and invoiced but still unpaid at your year end.
If a contractor took CIS tax off, enter the full amount before the deduction.
If turnover is £90,000 or more (or would be over a full year) you must use the full SA103F pages; below that you can use SA103S.
SA103F box 15; SA103S box 9.
If all your trading and miscellaneous income is £1,000 or less in total it is covered by the trading allowance and usually doesn't need reporting (not if it's from a connected party).
examples_allowed: Day rate invoiced against a client PO
Overtime, travel-day and cancellation fees
Per diems or expense reimbursements a client pays you
Kit hire you charge a client as part of your service
A fee paid in a foreign currency (converted to pounds)
examples_not_allowed: Money you put into the business yourself, or a loan
Refunds from suppliers (reduce the expense instead)
Wages from a PAYE job (they go on the employment pages)
Transfers between your own accounts
Income from a different trade (it needs its own self-employment pages)
evidence_to_keep: Every invoice, with PO number, client, date and amount
Remittance advices and bank statements showing the money in
CIS payment and deduction statements, if any
Self-billing statements from clients, if any
watch_out: Check that every invoice raised is in your records before you file.
If a client reimburses an expense, don't leave the reimbursement out of income and still claim the cost.
Foreign-currency fees must be converted to pounds (see foreign_currency).

other_income.title: Other business income
other_income.summary: This is trading income that isn't part of your normal fees, such as rent from letting part of your business premises. It is still taxable. It goes in SA103F box 16 (SA103S box 10).
rules: Use it for trading income not included in turnover, for example income from letting part of your business accommodation.
If you are VAT-registered, use the cash basis and keep figures including VAT, put any net VAT repayment from HMRC here.
Income from another trade goes on separate self-employment pages, not here.
The £1,000 trading allowance is claimed in SA103F box 16.1 instead of expenses. You can't claim both, and it can't create a loss.
examples_allowed: Net VAT repayment received (cash basis with VAT-inclusive figures)
Rent from sub-letting part of a business storage unit
examples_not_allowed: Income from a separate business
Personal gifts or money from family
Your normal fees (they go in turnover)
evidence_to_keep: Letter, statement or agreement showing what the payment was for
Bank record of the receipt
watch_out: Ask an accountant: one-off receipts such as insurance or compensation payouts can be taxable trading income or capital; get advice on how to treat them.

cost_of_goods.title: Cost of goods bought for resale or goods used
cost_of_goods.summary: The cost of goods you sell on, or use up in a job you charge for, is allowable. For crew work this is usually small. It goes in SA103F box 17 (SA103S box 11).
rules: Allowable: goods for resale, raw materials and direct costs of producing what you sell.
Not allowable: goods or materials bought for private use.
Cash basis: claim when you pay. Traditional accounting: adjust for opening and closing stock.
If you take stock out for your own use, add it back (SA103F box 60).
examples_allowed: Items you buy to sell on to a client
Parts or consumables bought for one client job and charged on to that client
examples_not_allowed: Things you buy for yourself
Tools and kit you keep using for years (see equipment)
Depreciation of equipment
evidence_to_keep: Supplier invoice or receipt with date, supplier, item and amount
The job or PO it was used on, if recharged
watch_out: Kit you keep and reuse is equipment, not cost of goods.
If a client paid you back, the payment must be in turnover (or netted off), not ignored.

materials.title: Materials and consumables
materials.summary: Materials and consumables that you use up while working are allowable. On the tax return they are reported with cost of goods in SA103F box 17 (SA103S box 11).
rules: Allowable: raw materials and direct costs of the work you sell.
Not allowable: materials for private use.
Items you keep and use for 2 years or more are equipment, not materials.
examples_allowed: Gaffer tape, cable ties, batteries and gels used up on jobs
Fixings, cable ends and small parts used in repairs on site
Cleaning products for your work kit
examples_not_allowed: Household supplies
Long-life tools or kit (see equipment)
evidence_to_keep: Receipts or invoices
Note of the job they were used on if the cost is large or recharged
watch_out: Bulk-bought consumables used partly at home: claim only the business share.

subcontractors.title: Construction industry subcontractors (CIS)
subcontractors.summary: Payments to subcontractors for construction work are allowable. This box (SA103F box 18) is only for construction work. If you pay other crew for non-construction work, use freelancers instead.
rules: SA103F box 18 covers payments to subcontractors or anyone else for construction work.
If you take on subcontractors for construction work you may need to register as a contractor under the Construction Industry Scheme.
Payments for non-business work are not allowable.
Claim the payment before any CIS tax you deducted.
examples_allowed: Paying a subcontractor for construction work on a business job (check CIS applies)
examples_not_allowed: Building work at your home
Ordinary crew labour that isn't construction (use freelancers)
evidence_to_keep: Subcontractor invoices
CIS verification records, monthly returns and deduction statements
Bank payments
watch_out: Ask an accountant: whether any staging, rigging or set-building you subcontract counts as construction under CIS.
CIS has its own registration, verification and monthly return rules, with penalties.

staff.title: Staff costs (employees)
staff.summary: Wages, bonuses, pensions and employer's National Insurance for people you employ are allowable. What you pay yourself is not. It goes in SA103F box 19 (SA103S box 13).
rules: Allowable: salaries, wages, bonuses, pensions, benefits, agency fees, employer's NI and staff training.
Not allowable: your own salary, drawings, pension payments or National Insurance.
Not allowable: carers or domestic help, for example nannies.
Pay to a relative or friend is allowable only for real work at a commercial rate; anything above that can be disallowed.
Staff costs not paid within 9 months after the end of the accounting period are disallowable for that period.
examples_allowed: Wages for an assistant employed through PAYE
Employer's NI on those wages
Agency fees for temporary staff
examples_not_allowed: Money you pay yourself
Paying a partner well above the going rate for little work
Childcare
evidence_to_keep: Payroll records and payslips
Timesheets or job records, especially for family members
Bank payments
watch_out: Ask an accountant: paying a family member needs real work, a sensible rate and actual payment.
If you employ anyone you'll normally need to run PAYE.

freelancers.title: Freelancers and other crew you pay
freelancers.summary: Paying other self-employed crew to help on jobs you have been booked for is allowable. These payments go in SA103F box 19 as subcontract labour, not box 18, which is for construction only.
rules: Allowable when you engage them for your business, for example you supply a two-person crew and pay the second person.
SA103F box 19 includes subcontract labour costs not included elsewhere.
Get an invoice from them for every job.
Only claim what you actually paid. If the client pays them directly, it isn't your cost.
examples_allowed: Paying a fellow technician you bring in on a job
Paying a driver to deliver your kit to a venue
examples_not_allowed: Paying someone for a personal favour
Crew the client books and pays directly
evidence_to_keep: Their invoice with name, dates, job and amount
Bank transfer record
The PO or job reference it relates to
watch_out: Ask an accountant: if someone works regularly for you under your direction, check whether they are really an employee for tax.

travel.title: Travel (general)
travel.summary: Business travel is allowable, but travel between home and a permanent or regular workplace (commuting) is not. If your home is your business base and you work at a series of temporary venues, travel from home to those venues is normally allowable.
rules: Allowable: train, bus, tram, air and taxi fares; hotel rooms and meals on overnight business trips; parking; vehicle hire.
Not allowable: non-business travel, fines and travel between home and work.
A journey with any private purpose is a dual-purpose journey and is not allowable. You can't split it.
Itinerant traders: where home is the base and work sites are temporary and change, home-to-site travel is normally allowable.
If you travel to one regular, predictable place (for example a hire company's warehouse every day), HMRC may treat it as your base, making home-to-there commuting.
Stopping on the way (for example at a supplier) doesn't turn a commute into a business journey.
SA103F box 20; SA103S box 12.
examples_allowed: Train to a venue for a load-in
Taxi from the venue to your hotel after a late load-out
Flight to an overseas show
examples_not_allowed: Travel for a holiday added on to a job
Daily journeys to a fixed regular workplace
Parking or speeding fines
evidence_to_keep: Tickets and receipts
Booking confirmations
Call sheet or schedule showing venue and times
The job or PO each trip relates to
watch_out: Ask an accountant: a long run at one venue, or regularly reporting to one client's base, can turn the trip from home into commuting.
The 24-month and 40% temporary workplace rules are employee rules; HMRC's business manual doesn't use them for the self-employed (see travel_rules).

travel_accommodation.title: Hotels and overnight accommodation
travel_accommodation.summary: When a job means you have to stay away from home overnight, the hotel and reasonable meals are allowable. Accommodation at your business base, or for private reasons, is not.
rules: Allowable where a business trip needs one or more nights away from home.
Reasonable meal costs taken with the overnight stay are allowable, whether or not they're on the hotel bill.
Not allowable: accommodation at your base of operations, even if a contract says you must live there.
The night before an early call, or after a late finish, at a distant venue can be part of the business trip if it's really needed.
Costs for a partner or family travelling with you are not allowable.
Extra nights for a holiday are private.
examples_allowed: Hotel near a venue 150 miles from home for a three-day build
Budget hotel the night before a 6am load-in far from home
Hotel after a 1am load-out when driving home would be unsafe
examples_not_allowed: Your partner's share of the room
Extra weekend nights for sightseeing
Rent on a flat near a place you work at permanently
evidence_to_keep: Itemised hotel invoice
Call sheet or schedule showing call and wrap times
A short note of why the stay was needed
watch_out: Ask an accountant: long stays at one location (weeks or months) may mean it has become your base.
If the client books and pays the hotel, don't claim it.
Only reasonable costs are allowed.

travel_rail.title: Train, tube, bus and tram fares
travel_rail.summary: Public transport fares for business journeys are allowable. Fares for commuting to a regular workplace, and personal trips, are not.
rules: Allowable for business journeys, for example home to a temporary venue, venue to venue, or to a client meeting.
Not allowable for travel between home and a permanent or regular base.
If one ticket covers business and private travel, only a clearly business journey is allowable; dual-purpose journeys are not.
SA103F box 20; SA103S box 12.
examples_allowed: Return rail ticket to a festival site you're crewing
Tube fares between two venues on the same day
examples_not_allowed: A season ticket to a regular workplace
Fares for a day out
evidence_to_keep: Tickets, e-tickets or booking confirmations
Contactless or Oyster journey history
Job or PO reference for each trip
watch_out: Mark personal journeys on your journey history so they aren't claimed by mistake.

travel_taxi.title: Taxis and ride-hailing
travel_taxi.summary: Taxi fares for business journeys are allowable. Taxis for private trips, for commuting to a regular workplace, or as part of entertaining clients are not.
rules: Allowable on business journeys, for example hotel to venue, or venue to station after a late finish.
Not allowable for travel between home and a permanent or regular base.
Travel that is part of entertaining clients (for example taking a client to dinner) is not allowable.
SA103F box 20; SA103S box 12.
examples_allowed: Taxi from a venue to your hotel after load-out
Taxi carrying kit to a temporary venue
examples_not_allowed: Taxi home from a night out
Taxi with a client to a restaurant
evidence_to_keep: Receipt or app trip record showing date, route and fare
Job or PO reference
watch_out: Ride-hailing apps mix personal and work trips; tag business trips as you go.

travel_local.title: Local travel
travel_local.summary: Short local journeys for work, such as getting between venues, suppliers or client meetings, are allowable. Local trips that are commuting or personal are not.
rules: Allowable when the journey is wholly for business.
Not allowable for travel from home to a regular place of work, or for private errands.
A business stop on a private or commuting journey doesn't make it a business journey.
SA103F box 20; SA103S box 12.
examples_allowed: Bus to a supplier to collect a part for a job
Hire bike or e-scooter between two venues
examples_not_allowed: Trip to the shops
Daily journey to a regular base
evidence_to_keep: Receipts or app records
A note of the purpose of each trip
watch_out: Small amounts add up; record them as you go rather than estimating at year end.

travel_flights.title: Flights
travel_flights.summary: Flights for business trips, such as working on an overseas show, are allowable. If a trip is partly a holiday, HMRC can refuse the whole travel cost.
rules: Allowable when the trip is wholly for business.
If a trip has a dual purpose (business and holiday), the travel cost is disallowed entirely.
Accommodation and meals abroad while you are working there for the business are allowable; holiday days are not.
Costs of a partner or family travelling with you are not allowable.
SA103F box 20; SA103S box 12.
examples_allowed: Flight to a European tour date you are booked on
Baggage fee for carrying work kit
examples_not_allowed: Your partner's flight
Flight for a holiday that includes a short meeting
evidence_to_keep: Booking confirmation and e-ticket
The booking or PO for the overseas job
Boarding passes
watch_out: Ask an accountant: if you extend a work trip for leisure, get advice before claiming the flight.

travel_parking.title: Parking, tolls and congestion charges
travel_parking.summary: Parking, tolls and congestion charges on business journeys are allowable, and you can claim them on top of the mileage flat rate. Parking at a regular workplace you commute to, and any fines, are not.
rules: Allowable on business journeys, including when you use the simplified mileage rate.
Not allowable where the journey is home to a permanent or regular workplace.
Fines and penalty charges are never allowable (see travel_penalties).
SA103F box 20; SA103S box 12.
examples_allowed: Venue or car park charges during a load-in
Bridge or road tolls driving to a job
Congestion charge driving kit into central London for a job
examples_not_allowed: Parking near a regular workplace
Parking or bus-lane penalty notices
evidence_to_keep: Parking receipts or app records
Toll and congestion charge receipts
Matching entry in your mileage log
watch_out: Keep parking costs separate from fines in your records.

travel_mileage.title: Mileage (simplified flat rate)
travel_mileage.summary: Instead of claiming the actual costs of your own car or van, you can claim a flat rate for each business mile. For 2026-27 the rate is 55p a mile for the first 10,000 miles and 25p after that; it was 45p and 25p before 6 April 2026.
rules: Cars and vans: 45p a mile for the first 10,000 business miles and 25p after, up to 2025-26.
Cars and vans: 55p a mile for the first 10,000 and 25p after, for 2026-27 (in law: Taxation (Energy and Vehicles) Act 2026).
Announced at Budget 2026, not yet law: the rate above 10,000 miles rises from 25p to 35p from 6 April 2027.
Motorcycles: 24p a mile, with no 10,000-mile band.
The 10,000 miles counts the total business miles in all cars and vans you claim on the flat rate in the period.
The flat rate replaces fuel, insurance, repairs, servicing, road tax, MOT and depreciation. Don't claim those as well.
You can still claim parking, tolls and congestion charges on business journeys.
Once you use the flat rate for a vehicle you must keep using it while that vehicle is in the business.
You can't use the flat rate for a vehicle you've claimed capital allowances on, or (cash basis) whose cost you deducted.
Only business journeys count, not commuting or private trips.
The flat rate is for cars, goods vehicles and motorcycles. Bicycles aren't covered; claim actual costs instead.
There is no extra amount for carrying passengers.
examples_allowed: Driving from home to a temporary venue and back (itinerant work)
Driving between two venues on the same day
Driving to a supplier to collect kit for a job
examples_not_allowed: Driving to a regular base you attend daily
Private trips
Miles in a hire car whose fuel you also claim
evidence_to_keep: A mileage log made at the time: date, start and end, purpose or job/PO, miles
Odometer readings at the start and end of each tax year
Call sheets or bookings that match the trips
watch_out: Decide flat rate or actual costs when the vehicle first goes into the business; you can't switch until you change vehicle.
A log written up from memory at year end is weak evidence.
Ask an accountant: if you use more than one car or van, or a hire car, check how the flat rate applies.

travel_car_hire.title: Car and van hire
travel_car_hire.summary: Hire charges for a vehicle used on business journeys are allowable. For longer hires or leases of cars with CO2 above 50g/km, 15% of the cost is disallowed under traditional accounting.
rules: Allowable: hire charges for business use; claim the fuel separately as an actual cost.
Short hires of 45 consecutive days or less are not restricted.
Longer car hires or leases (from 6 April 2021) with CO2 over 50g/km: disallow 15% of the hire cost (traditional accounting).
The 15% restriction doesn't apply on the cash basis.
Any private use of the hire vehicle must be taken out.
SA103F box 20; SA103S box 12.
examples_allowed: Van hired for a week to move your kit to a festival
Car hired at the airport for an overseas job
examples_not_allowed: Hire car used for a holiday
Fines charged to you by the hire company
evidence_to_keep: Hire agreement and invoice showing dates
Fuel receipts
Mileage or journey record for the hire period
watch_out: Don't claim mileage at the flat rate for the same journeys in a hire vehicle as well as hire and fuel.
Fines passed on by the hire company are not allowable (see travel_penalties).

travel_fuel.title: Fuel and charging
travel_fuel.summary: Fuel or electric charging for business journeys is allowable if you claim actual vehicle costs. If you use the mileage flat rate for that vehicle you can't also claim its fuel.
rules: Actual costs method: claim the business share of fuel for your own vehicle, based on business miles as a share of total miles.
Flat rate method: fuel is included in the rate, so claim nothing extra for that vehicle.
Fuel for a hire vehicle used on business is allowable.
Fuel for private and commuting trips is not allowable.
SA103F box 20; SA103S box 12.

Fuel for a hire van used to move kit to a job
examples_not_allowed: Fuel for your car when you claim 55p a mile for it
Fuel for family trips
evidence_to_keep: Fuel receipts
Mileage log showing business and total miles
watch_out: On actual costs you need total and business mileage to work out the business share.

travel_subsistence.title: Meals and subsistence when travelling
travel_subsistence.summary: Food is normally a private cost, but HMRC allows reasonable meals when you are travelling for work in an itinerant trade, on occasional trips outside your normal pattern, or on overnight stays. Routine daily lunches at a regular local workplace are not allowable.
rules: Allowable: reasonable meal costs on an overnight business trip.

Allowable: reasonable food and drink while travelling in the course of the trade, if the travel is allowable and the trade is itinerant at the time, or the trip is occasional and outside your normal pattern.
Not allowable: meals at your normal base, or routine lunches near a regular local site.
No part of a disallowed meal can be claimed as the 'extra cost' of eating out.
The self-employed claim actual, reasonable costs. HMRC's business manual gives no flat daily rates for the self-employed.
SA103F box 20 (overnight meals); other meals are disallowable.
examples_allowed: Evening meal during a two-night stay for an out-of-town show
Breakfast at a service station while driving to a distant venue
Food bought on a long travel day to a temporary site
examples_not_allowed: Lunch every day near a warehouse you work at regularly
Meals with friends
Food on days you're not travelling for work
evidence_to_keep: Receipts made at the time
Call sheet or job record showing you were travelling
Note of the trip it belongs to
watch_out: Ask an accountant: subsistence on day trips depends on the facts; HMRC may challenge regular daily meals.
If the client provides catering or pays a per diem, record the per diem as income and claim only real extra costs.

travel_penalties.title: Fines and penalty charges
travel_penalties.summary: Fines and penalty charges are never allowable, even if you got them while working. This includes parking tickets, speeding fines and bus-lane or congestion charge penalties.
rules: GOV.UK lists fines or penalty charges as costs you can't claim.
A penalty intended as punishment is not allowable.
SA103F treats fines as disallowable (box 35 if included in box 20).
examples_not_allowed: Parking ticket at a venue
Speeding fine on the way to a job
Penalty for not paying a congestion or clean air zone charge on time
evidence_to_keep: Record them separately so they aren't claimed by mistake
watch_out: The congestion charge itself is allowable on a business trip; the penalty for not paying it is not.

premises.title: Business premises (rent, rates, power)
premises.summary: Rent, business rates, power and security for premises used for the business, such as a lock-up or storage unit for your kit, are allowable. Buying premises, and private use of premises, are not. It goes in SA103F box 21 (SA103S box 14).

Not allowable: the cost of buying premises, or any non-business part of them.
Home costs go under use_of_home (business share or flat rate).

Electricity for a workshop where you maintain kit
examples_not_allowed: Storage of personal belongings in the same unit
Deposit or purchase price of a building

Utility and rates bills
watch_out: If a unit holds personal items too, claim only the business share.

insurance.title: Business insurance
insurance.summary: Insurance taken out for the business is allowable, such as public liability, professional indemnity, kit insurance and business vehicle cover. Insurance on your own life or health is not.
rules: Allowable: public liability and other business insurance, professional indemnity premiums, and insurance on business equipment.
Vehicle insurance is part of car, van and travel costs (not if you use the mileage flat rate).

Private use: reduce the claim by the private use share (for example a laptop used half privately: claim half).

wholly_and_exclusively.title: Wholly and exclusively (duality and apportionment)
wholly_and_exclusively.summary: A cost is allowable only if it is spent wholly and exclusively for the business. If a cost has two purposes that can't be separated, none of it is allowable. If a clear business part can be identified, that part is allowable.
rules: The law (ITTOIA 2005 s34) blocks any cost not incurred wholly and exclusively for the trade.
Dual purpose: if one cost serves business and private purposes at once and can't be split, disallow it all (for example a holiday with a short meeting).
Apportionment: where a definite part of a cost is for business, that part is allowable (for example business miles, business calls, a room used for work).
Use a reasonable method, such as a representative sample period, and keep using it until things change.
Some costs always have a private purpose built in, such as everyday clothes, ordinary meals and home-to-work travel.
The test is about purpose, judged from the facts and evidence, not just what you say you intended.
What you do with profits after earning them (drawings, paying tax) isn't an expense.

travel_rules.title: Travel rules for a self-employed crew member
travel_rules.summary: Business travel is allowable but ordinary commuting is not. If your home is your business base and you travel to a series of temporary venues, that travel is normally allowable. The employee 24-month and 40% rules don't formally apply to you; the test is your base of operations and whether the trip has a private purpose.
rules: Home to a permanent or regular place of work is commuting and not allowable.
Itinerant trade: if you move from home to a series of temporary jobs, and home is your base, home-to-site travel is normally allowable (Horton v Young).
Predictability matters: going to a fixed, regular place points to that place being your base (Powell v Jackman).
Doing admin at home or keeping tools there doesn't by itself make home your base.
Travel between work sites, and from your base to a temporary site, is business travel.
Very long distances can still be questioned (HMRC's example of someone living in London working only in Cornwall).
24-month and 40% rules: these are in employee law (ITEPA s339). HMRC's Business Income Manual does not use them for traders.
Meals: allowable when travelling in the course of an itinerant trade, on occasional trips outside your normal pattern, or with an overnight stay; only reasonable amounts.
Overnight stays: hotel and reasonable meals are allowable when the trip needs a night away; not at your base.
Night before or after: allowable when genuinely needed for the job (early call or late finish far from home).
Trips mixed with a holiday: the travel cost can be disallowed in full.
Keep records made at the time: mileage log, receipts, call sheets.
Ask an accountant: long runs at one venue, regular work at one client's base, or long stays away can change whether travel and hotels are allowable.

use_of_home.title: Use of home: flat rate or actual share
use_of_home.summary: You can claim home running costs either with a monthly flat rate based on hours worked at home, or as a reasonable share of actual bills. You can't use both, and phone and internet are claimed separately either way.
rules: Flat rate needs 25 hours or more of business work at home in the month.
Flat rates: 25-50 hours £10 a month; 51-100 hours £18; 101+ hours £26.
Actual share: split costs by a reasonable method, such as rooms used and time.
Fixed costs (Council Tax, mortgage interest, rent, insurance) need part of the home used solely for business for a period.
Running costs (heating, lighting) follow actual business usage.
Mortgage capital repayments are not allowable.
Small claims for light use (for example paperwork) can be on any reasonable basis.
Phone and internet: business share as an actual cost on top.

trading_allowance.title: Trading allowance (£1,000)
trading_allowance.summary: The trading allowance gives up to £1,000 of trading income tax-free each year. If your income is higher, you can deduct the £1,000 instead of your actual expenses, but not both. For a full-time freelancer, claiming actual expenses is almost always better.
rules: Gross trading income of £1,000 or less in a tax year: usually no need to tell HMRC.
Above £1,000: choose either the £1,000 allowance or your actual expenses and capital allowances.
It can be split across more than one trade and miscellaneous income, but the total is £1,000.
It can't be used to create a loss.
It can't be used for income from your employer, or from a company or partnership you (or a connected person) own or control.

cash_basis.title: Cash basis (default from 2024-25)
cash_basis.summary: From 6 April 2024 the cash basis is the default for sole traders. You record income when you're paid and expenses when you pay them. You can opt out and use traditional (accruals) accounting by ticking a box on your return.
rules: Income counts when received; expenses when paid.
Most equipment (including vans) is deducted as an expense when paid; cars still get capital allowances (or the mileage rate).
Not deductible on the cash basis: cars, land, assets that won't lose 90% of value within 20 years, items not for continuing use, education or training as capital.
No bad debt relief, because unpaid invoices are never counted as income.
From 2024-25: no turnover limit, no £500 interest cap, and losses get the same reliefs as under traditional accounting.
The 15% car hire restriction doesn't apply on the cash basis.
To opt out, choose traditional accounting and tick SA103F box 10; you may need transitional adjustments when you switch.
Traditional may suit you if a lender wants accounts or you have high stock or large unpaid invoices at year end.
Who can't use it includes companies, LLPs and partnerships with a company partner.

by_year.2023-24: Opt-in only. Entry limit £150,000 turnover; leave above £300,000. Interest capped at £500. Cash basis losses couldn't be set against other income.
by_year.2024-25: Default for eligible sole traders; opt out to use traditional accounting. Turnover limits, £500 interest cap and loss restrictions removed.

capital_allowances.title: Capital allowances
capital_allowances.summary: Capital allowances give tax relief for kit and vehicles you buy and keep. On the cash basis you only need them for cars. On traditional accounting most equipment gets the Annual Investment Allowance (AIA) of up to £1 million, and cars go into pools based on their CO2 emissions.
rules: AIA: £1 million a year; full relief for most plant and machinery, but not cars.
AIA can't be claimed on items you owned before using them in the business, or on gifts.
40% first-year allowance: new, unused main-rate items (not cars) bought on or after 1 January 2026.
Full expensing (100%) and the 50% special rate FYA are for companies only, not sole traders.
Main pool writing down allowance: 18% a year to 5 April 2026, 14% from 6 April 2026.
Special rate pool: 6% a year (integral features, long-life assets, cars over 50g/km).
Small pools: if a pool is £1,000 or less you can claim it all.
Cars bought from April 2021: new zero-emission or electric 100% first-year allowance (bought before April 2027); up to 50g/km main pool; over 50g/km special rate pool.
Private use: each mixed-use asset goes in its own single asset pool and the allowance is reduced by the private share.
Selling an asset can create a balancing charge (taxable) or balancing allowance.
Cash basis: capital allowances only for cars; other kit is deducted as an expense.
Can't claim capital allowances if you use the trading allowance.
Ask an accountant: mixed-use assets, cars, disposals, and switching between cash basis and traditional accounting.

losses.title: Trading losses
losses.summary: If your allowable costs are more than your income, you have a trading loss. You can use it to reduce tax on other income this year or last year, carry it forward against future profits from the same trade, or in the early years carry it back three years.
rules: Sideways relief: set the loss against total income of the loss year and/or the previous year (ITA 2007 s64).
Claim deadline for s64 and early years relief: 12 months after 31 January following the loss year (for a 2025-26 loss, 31 January 2028).
You can't choose a part amount: the loss is used as far as possible against that year's income.
Early years relief: losses in the first 4 tax years of a trade can be carried back against total income of the 3 previous years, earliest first (s72).
Carry forward: unused losses go against future profits of the same trade (s83). Make the claim within 4 years of the end of the loss year (usually on your return).
Terminal loss relief: loss in the final 12 months can go back against profits of the same trade for 3 years.
Cap: relief against other income is limited to the greater of £50,000 or 25% of adjusted total income; the cap doesn't apply against profits of the same trade.
Restrictions apply if you spend less than 10 hours a week on average on the trade, or it isn't run commercially with a view to profit.
Losses can also be set against capital gains after other income.
Ask an accountant: choosing which year to use a loss in, and the hours and commercial tests.

by_year.2023-24: Cash basis losses (2013-14 to 2023-24) could not be set against other income or carried back; carry forward only.
by_year.2024-25: Cash basis losses now get the same reliefs as traditional accounting.
by_year.2025-26: Same as 2024-25. For a 2025-26 loss, early years carry-back is only available if the business began after 5 April 2022.
by_year.2026-27: Same rules; cap still £50,000 or 25% of adjusted total income.

payments_on_account.title: Payments on account
payments_on_account.summary: Payments on account are two advance payments towards next year's tax, each usually half of last year's bill. They are due on 31 January and 31 July. If you expect a lower bill, you can ask to reduce them.
rules: Two payments, due 31 January (in the tax year) and 31 July (after it), each normally half of last year's Self Assessment tax including Class 4 NI.
Not needed if last year's Self Assessment bill was under £1,000, or more than 80% of your tax was already paid at source (for example through PAYE).
The balancing payment (what's left) is due by 31 January after the tax year, along with the first payment on account for the next year.
First year: your first January bill can include the whole of last year's tax plus half again as the first payment on account.
Reduce them online in your Self Assessment account or with form SA303 if you expect lower profits.
If you reduce them too far, HMRC charges interest on the shortfall.
Payments on account are tax, not a business expense.

by_year.2026-27: Same rules. Announced at Budget 2026: from April 2029, people who make payments on account will move to smaller, more regular automated in-year payments (details not yet confirmed).

national_insurance.title: National Insurance (Class 2 and Class 4)
national_insurance.summary: Self-employed people pay Class 4 NI on profits above £12,570. Since April 2024 you no longer have to pay Class 2; if your profits are at or above the Small Profits Threshold it's treated as paid so your State Pension record is protected. Below that, you can pay Class 2 voluntarily.
rules: Class 4 is worked out on your profits and paid through Self Assessment with your income tax.
Class 4 lower profits limit £12,570 and upper profits limit £50,270 (2023-24 to 2026-27).
Class 2 (from 2024-25): not payable; treated as paid if profits are at or above the Small Profits Threshold.
Below the Small Profits Threshold you can pay voluntary Class 2 to protect your State Pension and benefits.
You must be registered as self-employed for Class 2 to be treated as paid or to pay voluntarily.
Class 4 isn't due if you reached State Pension age before the start of the tax year.
NI is not a business expense.

by_year.2024-25: Class 4: 6% on £12,570-£50,270, 2% above. Class 2: no longer payable; treated as paid if profits £6,725 or more; voluntary rate £3.45 a week.

personal_allowance_taper.title: Personal Allowance taper (£100,000 to £125,140)
personal_allowance_taper.summary: Your £12,570 Personal Allowance is reduced by £1 for every £2 of adjusted net income over £100,000, and is gone at £125,140. In that band each extra £1 of income effectively costs 60p in income tax (40% plus the lost allowance), before NI. Pension contributions and Gift Aid reduce adjusted net income and can restore the allowance.
rules: Personal Allowance £12,570 for 2023-24 to 2026-27, and frozen to 2030-31.
Taper: lose £1 of allowance for every £2 of adjusted net income above £100,000; nil at £125,140.

Adjusted net income: taxable income minus trading losses and gross pension contributions paid without relief, minus grossed-up Gift Aid and relief-at-source pension contributions (£1.25 for each £1 paid).
Effective marginal income tax rate in the taper band is 60% (plus 2% Class 4 NI on profits above £50,270).
Rates (England, Wales, NI): basic 20% on the first £37,700 above the allowance, higher 40% up to £125,140, additional 45% above.
Scotland has different bands and rates.

by_year.2023-24: PA £12,570; taper from £100,000; additional rate threshold £125,140.
by_year.2026-27: Same; Budget 2025 froze the PA and basic rate limit to 2030-31.

pension_contributions.title: Pension contributions
pension_contributions.summary: Paying into a personal pension gets tax relief. With relief at source you pay £80 and the provider adds £20. If you pay higher-rate tax, your basic rate band is extended by the gross contribution, giving extra relief, and the contribution also reduces adjusted net income for the £100,000 taper.
rules: Relief at source: the provider claims 20% basic rate relief and adds it to your pot.
Higher or additional rate: claim the extra relief on your Self Assessment return.
How: the basic rate limit and higher rate limit are increased by the gross contribution.
Relief is limited to the higher of 100% of your UK taxable earnings or £3,600 gross a year.
Annual allowance £60,000, with unused allowance carried forward from the previous 3 years if conditions are met.
Tapered annual allowance if threshold income is over £200,000 and adjusted income over £260,000 (minimum £10,000).
Money purchase annual allowance £10,000 if you have flexibly accessed a pension.
Gross relief-at-source contributions reduce adjusted net income, which can restore the Personal Allowance above £100,000.
Personal pension contributions are not a business expense; they're claimed on the main return.

by_year.2023-24: Annual allowance £60,000; MPAA £10,000; taper threshold income £200,000, adjusted income £260,000.

gift_aid.title: Gift Aid

Charity donations are not a business expense.

marriage_allowance.title: Marriage Allowance
marriage_allowance.summary: If you're married or in a civil partnership and one of you earns less than the Personal Allowance, they can transfer £1,260 of it to the other, who must be a basic rate taxpayer. This saves up to £252 a year.

vat_registration.title: VAT registration
vat_registration.summary: You must register for VAT if your taxable turnover over the last 12 months goes over £90,000, or you expect it to in the next 30 days. You can register voluntarily below that. For a freelancer working mostly for VAT-registered production companies, voluntary registration can let you reclaim VAT on kit and costs without costing clients more.
rules: Threshold: £90,000 from 1 April 2024 (£85,000 before). Deregistration threshold £88,000 (£83,000 before).
Rolling test: register within 30 days of the end of the month you went over.
Future test: register if you expect to go over £90,000 in the next 30 days alone.
Voluntary registration is allowed below the threshold.
Pros: reclaim VAT on business purchases; VAT-registered clients can usually reclaim the VAT you charge.
Cons: you must charge VAT on your sales, file VAT returns and keep VAT records; it raises prices for clients who aren't VAT-registered.
After registering you can reclaim VAT on goods bought up to 4 years before (if you still have them) and services up to 6 months before.
No VAT reclaim on business entertainment; partial reclaim for mixed-use items.
Flat Rate Scheme: join if expected taxable turnover is £150,000 or less (excluding VAT); leave above £230,000 (including VAT).
Flat Rate Scheme: limited cost businesses (goods under 2% of turnover, or under £1,000 a year) pay 16.5%, which often makes it poor value for labour-only crew.
Flat Rate Scheme sector examples: entertainment or journalism 12.5%; any other activity not listed 12%; film, radio, TV or video production 13%. 1% off in your first year of VAT registration.
Ask an accountant: whether voluntary registration or the Flat Rate Scheme suits your mix of clients and purchases, and which flat rate sector fits your work.

mtd_itsa.title: Making Tax Digital for Income Tax
mtd_itsa.summary: MTD for Income Tax means keeping digital records and sending HMRC quarterly updates from compatible software, then a tax return at year end. It started on 6 April 2026 for sole traders and landlords with qualifying income over £50,000, and widens to over £30,000 from April 2027 and over £20,000 from April 2028.
rules: Qualifying income is your total gross self-employment and property income before expenses (turnover).
Employment, partnership profit shares, dividends and pensions don't count.
The threshold is tested on an earlier year's tax return; HMRC writes to you, but it's your responsibility to check.
Quarterly updates cover the tax year to date: periods to 5 July, 5 October, 5 January and 5 April; deadlines 7 August, 7 November, 7 February and 7 May.

Updates are category totals, not individual receipts. No tax is paid with an update, but after each one you can see an estimate of your tax bill for the year so far in your software and your HMRC online account.
Corrections flow into the next update because each update is cumulative.
You still submit a tax return, and payment dates stay 31 January and 31 July.
Use HMRC-recognised software (bridging software if you use spreadsheets).
Late submission: 1 point per missed deadline; £200 penalty at 4 points.
No penalty points for late quarterly updates in your first MTD tax year.
You can opt out if qualifying income stays below the threshold for 3 tax years in a row.
Digital records must include amounts and dates of each transaction.

by_year.2025-26: Not in MTD yet. Your 2025-26 qualifying income decides whether you join from 6 April 2027 (over £30,000).
by_year.2026-27: Mandatory if 2024-25 qualifying income was over £50,000. First year: no points for late quarterly updates. Your 2026-27 income decides whether you join from April 2028 (over £20,000).
by_year.2027-28: Mandatory if 2025-26 qualifying income over £30,000. Budget 2026: no penalty points for late quarterly updates in 2027-28 for April 2027 joiners. MTD late payment penalties rise to 4% at day 15 and 4% at day 30, plus 10% a year from day 31.

record_keeping.title: Record keeping
record_keeping.summary: Keep records of all business income and expenses, and the evidence behind them, for at least 5 years after the 31 January filing deadline. Digital copies are acceptable if they're complete. Under MTD you must keep the records digitally in compatible software.
rules: Keep records of sales and income, business expenses, VAT and PAYE records if relevant, and personal income.
Evidence includes receipts, invoices, bank statements, and sales invoices or till records.
Keep them for at least 5 years after the 31 January submission deadline for that tax year.
If you file more than 4 years late, keep them for 15 months after you send the return.
Electronic copies (scans, photos) are fine if they are complete and full copies of the originals.
Some originals must be kept, such as certificates of tax deducted.
Penalty of up to £3,000 for failing to keep adequate records (normally only in serious cases).
If records are lost, use best estimates and tell HMRC the figures are estimated or provisional.
MTD: record each transaction's amount and date digitally, by the time the quarterly update is due.
Mileage logs, call sheets and POs help prove travel and subsistence claims.

client_rebilled_expenses.title: Recharging expenses to clients (recharges and disbursements)
client_rebilled_expenses.summary: If you pay a cost and bill it to your client, the cost is usually your expense and the amount billed is your income. If the client pays a supplier directly (for example books your hotel), it's not your income or your expense.
Per diems or buyouts paid to you are income; claim only your real allowable costs.

VAT disbursement: only when you pay as the client's agent, the client received the goods or services, the client was responsible for paying, agreed you could pay, knew of the supplier, it's shown separately at exact cost, and it's extra to your own services.
Your own travel, hotels and postage passed on to a client are recharges, not disbursements; charge VAT on them if you're VAT-registered.
Mark rechargeable costs against the PO so nothing is missed on the invoice.

foreign_currency.title: Foreign currency
foreign_currency.summary: Income and costs in other currencies must be converted into pounds for your records and tax return. HMRC accepts the rate in your accounts, a bank's rate, or HMRC's published monthly average rates. Use one sensible method consistently.
rules: Rates you can use include a bank's quoted rate, London closing rates, or HMRC's monthly average rates (published for VAT and customs).
HMRC's monthly rates are now published on the Trade Tariff exchange rates service (trade-tariff.service.gov.uk/exchange_rates).
HMRC only questions a rate that is markedly different from reputable sources.
Convert each amount using your chosen rate for the date (or month) it was received or paid, and use the same method every time.
Bank currency conversion fees are allowable finance costs.
Ask an accountant: exchange gains or losses on money held in foreign currency, and any foreign tax deducted from fees, need specialist treatment.

entertainment_and_gifts.title: Entertainment and gifts
entertainment_and_gifts.summary: Entertaining clients and suppliers is not allowable. Gifts are not allowable either, except small branded gifts costing no more than £50 per person per tax year that aren't food, drink, tobacco or vouchers.
rules: Business entertainment and gifts are disallowed by law (ITTOIA s45), even if they help win work.
Entertaining employees, where they are the main attendees, is an exception.
Gift exception: carries a conspicuous advert for your business (on the item, not just the wrapping).
Gift exception: total gifts to the same person no more than £50 in the tax year.
Gift exception: not food, drink, tobacco or vouchers.
Free samples of what you sell and competition prizes open to the public can be allowable.
No VAT reclaim on entertaining.

clothing.title: Clothing
clothing.summary: Everyday clothes aren't allowable, even if you only wear them for work or a client insists. Protective gear, uniforms and costumes are allowable, including cleaning and repairing them.
rules: Allowable: safety boots, hard hats, hi-vis, protective gloves and overalls used only for work.
Allowable: specialist clothing or uniforms that aren't everyday clothing, and costumes.
Not allowable: suits, shirts, dresses, ordinary shoes, plain black work clothes.
Mallalieu v Drummond: clothes you could wear every day always have a private purpose (warmth and decency).

training.title: Training
training.summary: Training is allowable if it relates to your existing business, including updating skills, keeping up with new technology and learning related new skills. Training to start a new business or move into unrelated work is not.
rules: Allowable: improving skills you use now, keeping up with industry technology, new skills linked to changes in your industry, and admin skills like bookkeeping.
Not allowable: starting a new business, or expanding into areas not directly related to your industry.

late_filing_penalties_and_interest.title: Late filing penalties and interest (not allowable)
late_filing_penalties_and_interest.summary: Penalties and interest from HMRC are never allowable expenses. Filing and paying on time is the only way to avoid them.
rules: Late return: £100 at once; after 3 months £10 a day (up to £900); after 6 and 12 months a further 5% of the tax due or £300, whichever is more.
Late payment (Self Assessment): 5% of unpaid tax at 30 days, 6 months and 12 months.

MTD for Income Tax users: points-based late submission penalties and new late payment penalties (2026-27: 3% of tax owed at day 15, another 3% at day 30, then 10% a year; in your first year you get 30 days before penalties start).
Late payment interest: Bank of England base rate plus 4% (from 6 April 2025; was plus 2.5%).
HMRC late payment interest: 8.00% from 24 November 2026 (was 7.75% from 9 January 2026).
Interest and penalties on tax are not deductible in working out profits.
You can appeal a penalty if you have a reasonable excuse.

basis_period_reform.title: Basis period reform (tax year basis)
basis_period_reform.summary: From 2024-25 you are taxed on the profits of the tax year itself (6 April to 5 April), whatever your accounting date. 2023-24 was the transition year. If your year end isn't 31 March or 5 April you must apportion your accounts to the tax year.
rules: Accounting periods ending 31 March to 5 April are treated as matching the tax year.
Other year ends: apportion profits by days (or another reasonable, consistent method).
If final figures aren't ready by the deadline you may need to file provisional figures.
Transition profit from 2023-24 is spread over 5 years by default (2023-24 to 2027-28), or you can accelerate it.
Overlap relief was all used in 2023-24.
Transition profits count for Class 4 NI.

ways_to_reduce_tax_legally.title: Time equipment purchases sensibly
ways_to_reduce_tax_legally.how: On the cash basis, kit is deducted in the tax year you pay for it; on traditional accounting, AIA gives full relief in the year of purchase. If you need kit anyway, buying it before 5 April brings the relief into the earlier year.

ways_to_reduce_tax_legally.limits: Only buy what the business needs. Cars don't get AIA or the cash basis deduction. Private use reduces the claim. Selling the kit later can be taxable.

ways_to_reduce_tax_legally.title: Pay into a personal pension
ways_to_reduce_tax_legally.how: Pay into a relief-at-source personal pension: you pay £80, the provider adds £20. Higher-rate taxpayers claim extra relief on the return through an extended basic rate band.
